title: Sacral Neuromodulation for Refractory Endometriosis-Associated Chronic Pelvic Pain: A 12-Month Prospective Single-Arm Cohort Study
content: Background. Endometriosis-associated chronic pelvic pain (CPP) frequently persists despite hormonal suppression and excisional surgery, reflecting peripheral and central sensitization rather than lesion burden alone. Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) modulates sacral afferent traffic and has established efficacy in lower urinary tract and bowel dysfunction, but evidence in endometriosis-associated CPP is limited to small series.Objective. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of S3 sacral neuromodulation over 12 months in women with endometriosis-associated CPP refractory to medical and surgical treatment.Methods. Prospective, multicentre, single-arm cohort study (single treatment group; no control arm). Sixty-eight women were screened and 55 women aged 25–55 years with laparoscopically and histologically confirmed endometriosis and CPP of at least 6 months were enrolled. All had received guideline-based medical therapy (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, combined oral contraceptives, progestins, gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonists, or combinations) for at least 6 months, discontinued at least 3 months before implantation, and 38 had undergone prior excisional surgery. All 55 underwent staged S3 quadripolar lead test stimulation; those achieving at least 50% pain reduction proceeded to implantable pulse generator placement. The primary outcome was change in 10-point Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score from baseline to 12 months. Secondary outcomes were the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), a bladder-and-bowel symptom score, the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) physical and mental component scores, rescue analgesic use, and adverse events. Paired and independent-sample t-tests, McNemar’s test and Cohen’s d were used; p < 0.05 was considered significant.Results. Forty-five of 55 women (81.8%) responded to test stimulation, received a permanent device and completed 12-month follow-up; 10 (18.2%) did not achieve adequate trial relief and were not implanted. Mean VAS fell from 8.8 ± 0.9 to 1.8 ± 1.6 (mean change −7.0, 95% CI −7.50 to −6.50; t(44) = 28.4; p < 0.001; Cohen’s d_z = 4.2). Marked response (≥70% reduction) occurred in 30 of 45 (66.7%) and moderate response (30–69%) in 15 of 45 (33.3%). PCS, bladder-and-bowel and both SF-36 component scores improved significantly (all p < 0.001), and rescue analgesic use fell from 45 of 45 (100%) to 12 of 45 (26.7%; p < 0.001). No major device-related complications, infections, lead migrations or explanations occurred during 12 months.Conclusion. In this uncontrolled cohort, S3 sacral neuromodulation was associated with large, sustained reductions in pain and improvements in quality of life at 12 months, with a favourable safety profile, in carefully selected women with refractory endometriosis-associated CPP. Randomised, sham-controlled trials are required before causal efficacy can be claimed.
